theorem_title: Five-burn preparation of a line guard
natural_language_statement:
Starting with no blocked sites on a line, the Devil can prepare a blocked triple above a king in five burns, despite every intervening horizontal displacement being -1, 0, or 1.

The finite strategy predicate records four intervening moves and a final burn that completes the triple. This is the local preparation lemma used to guard a box boundary.
source: Martin Kutz, The Angel Problem, Positional Games, and Digraph Roots (2004), Chapter 1, Section 1.1, pp. 2-3, Figures 1-3. https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/alumni/d1/2009/mkutz/diss/kutz_angel.pdf. Finite strategy certificate for Figure 2; index 4 represents five burns.

theorem_title: Preservation of a guarded box against a chess king
formal_statement: theorem AngelDevil.king_box_step (p : AngelDevil.Point) (B : Finset AngelDevil.Point) (h : AngelDevil.KingBoxReady p B) : ∃ z ∈ AngelDevil.kingBoard, ∀ q, AngelDevil.Jump 1 p q → q ∉ insert z B → AngelDevil.KingBoxReady q (insert z B) := by sorry
natural_language_statement:
Suppose the king is strictly inside the box [-100,100]^2, its corner boundary segments are blocked, and each side has a line guard whose preparation fits the remaining distance. Then there is a single square in the box for the Devil to block such that every subsequent legal king move preserves these conditions.

This formal invariant implements the four-side confinement argument; the constants are deliberately loose, not an optimal capture bound.
source: Martin Kutz, The Angel Problem, Positional Games, and Digraph Roots (2004), Chapter 1, Section 1.1, pp. 2-3, Figures 1-3. https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/alumni/d1/2009/mkutz/diss/kutz_angel.pdf. Implementation of Figure 3 with radius 100 and seven-site corner arms, rather than the illustrated constants.

theorem_title: Winning Angel strategies are monotone in power
formal_statement: theorem AngelDevil.angelWins_mono {p q : Nat} (hpq : p ≤ q) (h : AngelDevil.AngelWins p) : AngelDevil.AngelWins q := by sorry
natural_language_statement:
For natural-number powers p ≤ q, if a single power-p Angel strategy survives against every Devil, then a power-q Angel has a winning strategy as well.

The game histories and Devil actions are unchanged when only the permitted jump radius increases.
source: Andras Mathe, The Angel of power 2 wins (2007), Theorem 4.6 and Section 1 game definition; https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548306008303. Elementary consequence of the Chebyshev jump rule, not a separately numbered theorem.

theorem_title: Every Angel of integer power at least two wins
formal_statement: theorem AngelDevil.power_ge_two_wins (p : Nat) (hp : 2 ≤ p) : AngelDevil.AngelWins p := by sorry
natural_language_statement:
For every integer power p ≥ 2, there exists one Angel strategy that survives forever against every ordinary Devil strategy on the infinite integer lattice.

The Devil burns at most one square per round; the convention is Devil first, with passing permitted. This is the monotonicity corollary of the power-two theorem.
source: Andras Mathe, The Angel of power 2 wins (2007), Theorem 4.6 and Section 1 game definition; https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548306008303. Monotonicity corollary of Theorem 4.6.

theorem_title: The Devil defeats the power-one Angel
formal_statement: theorem AngelDevil.power_one_devil_wins : ∃ D : AngelDevil.DevilStrategy, ∀ A, ¬ AngelDevil.Survives 1 A D := by sorry
natural_language_statement:
There exists a single ordinary Devil strategy that defeats every power-one Angel strategy on the infinite board. Defeat means a finite round with an illegal jump or a landing on an already burned square.

The quantifier order is one Devil strategy against all Angel strategies, not a separate opponent chosen after each Angel strategy. The model allows the Angel to stay still and the Devil to burn the occupied square; only subsequent landings lose.
source: Martin Kutz, The Angel Problem, Positional Games, and Digraph Roots (2004), Chapter 1, Section 1.1, pp. 2-3, Figures 1-3. https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/alumni/d1/2009/mkutz/diss/kutz_angel.pdf. Berlekamp chess-king capture argument. Formal implementation uses 56 preparatory burns in a radius-100 box, followed by finite exhaustion; no optimal deadline claimed.

theorem_title: Complete classification by integer Angel power
formal_statement: theorem AngelDevil.angelWins_iff_two_le (p : Nat) : AngelDevil.AngelWins p ↔ 2 ≤ p := by sorry
natural_language_statement:
In the standard infinite-board game against a Devil that burns at most one square per round, the Angel has a winning strategy exactly for natural-number powers p ≥ 2.

The negative cases are p=0 and p=1. The zero-power case is included because the formal parameter ranges over all natural numbers. This combines the known king-capture result with Mathe's power-two theorem and monotonicity.
source: Martin Kutz, The Angel Problem, Positional Games, and Digraph Roots (2004), Chapter 1, Section 1.1, pp. 2-3, Figures 1-3. https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/alumni/d1/2009/mkutz/diss/kutz_angel.pdf. Andras Mathe, The Angel of power 2 wins (2007), Theorem 4.6 and Section 1 game definition; https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548306008303. Logical combination of these published results.
